abstract: This Master's dissertation (Federal University of Bahia, 2021), authored by Helen Fernandes Sousa under the supervision of André Lemos, investigates whether the use of digital platforms alters the work relations and practices of self-employed professional tattoo artists who use Instagram professionally. Drawing on a neo-materialist framework, it describes Instagram's tools, materialities and algorithmic performativity, then examines through autoethnography and a 590-respondent survey how platform use reshapes tattooing work. It concludes that Instagram use generates dependence and modifies the social profile of workers, their workspace, procedures, unpaid work hours, and may transform tattoo artists into influencers and products.
key_claims: The use of Instagram 'tattoos the tattooers' — it adds new tasks to professional routines, alters temporal regimes, modifies the tattooing procedure, reconfigures the workspace and changes the profile of tattoo artists.
Agency is not solely human: digital platforms, through their materiality and algorithmic performativity, co-produce and modify the social world of work.

Even professions that predate and do not originally depend on platforms (such as tattooing) can become so intertwined with platform use that they fit the concept of platformized labor, generating dependence.
The author proposes extending existing typologies of platformized labor to include freelance professionals who use digital social networks (like Instagram) as work platforms.
Platform use introduces symptoms of labor precarization, including dependence and many hours of unpaid work folded into professionals' routines, often blurred with leisure.
methods: Neo-materialist (less anthropocentric) methodology for social studies of communication, drawing on Lemos, Alldred & Fox, and Coole & Frost.
Descriptive analysis of Instagram's interface, tools, resources, account types, materialities and algorithmic functioning.
Autoethnography: critical self-analysis of the author's own work as a tattoo artist and heavy Instagram user, analyzing data from her professional account over a defined period.
Online survey (questionnaire) with 590 professional tattoo artists about their Instagram use and perceptions of how the platform shapes their professional practice.
Triangulation comparing survey results with the autoethnographic findings and the theoretical literature.
findings: Platform use produces dependence among tattoo artists, who rely on Instagram to be found by potential clients.
It modifies the social profile of workers, the workspace (making it 'Instagrammable'), activities and procedures, and the aesthetic/artistic creation.
It adds substantial unpaid work hours (feeding the portfolio, communicating with potential clients, learning the platform) that are often unmeasured or perceived as leisure.
Success depends on 'playing the platform game' — adapting practices (e.g., image formats, branding) to Instagram's materiality and algorithmic performativity.
Tattoo artists may be transformed into digital influencers and into products themselves, and brands increasingly hire them for advertising.
Survey results largely matched the autoethnographic perceptions and revealed some unexpected results indicating changes in the tattoo field tied to platform use.
contributions: Extends the concept of platformization of labor and existing typologies (Grohmann; Graham & Woodcock; Casilli & Posada; Schmidt; Scholz) to freelance workers using digital social networks as de facto work platforms.
Provides an empirical case study (autoethnography plus a 590-respondent survey) of platform effects on an occupation not originally designed around platforms.
Offers a neo-materialist analytic model for studying how platforms 'make-do' (fazer-fazer) and reshape self-employed work.
Documents concrete mechanisms of labor precarization (dependence, unpaid labor, surveillance) among independent creative professionals in Brazil.
Serves as a methodological and conceptual basis for future studies on how digital platforms affect diverse professional fields.
framing: The dissertation positions itself within neo-materialist social studies of communication and the literature on the platformization of labor, extending debates about 'uberization,' algorithmic management and digital influencers to self-employed creative workers. It foregrounds non-anthropocentric agency, treating Instagram as an active participant that co-produces professional practice.
